analysis.title: Public Finances: Under the pressure of rising interest rates (Ecopulse, November 2026)
key_insights: Fiscal policies diverge: the US public deficit is projected to widen to nearly 9% of GDP by 2032 (federal deficit 7.2%) because there is no effort to improve the primary balance. Germany (investment plans) and Japan (pro-growth policies) also see deficits rise.

The UK and France are expected to keep consolidating and return to a primary surplus before 2030, with a greater risk of deviation from the central scenario in France. Italy and Spain deficits are expected to stay below 3% of GDP.

Interest payments rise in every country in the sample by 2032 as low-rate debt is refinanced. France's payments double by 2032 and approach Italy's level. Germany and Japan more than double from low levels. The US reaches the highest level in the sample at 5% of GDP.
The gap between the apparent interest rate and nominal growth becomes unfavourable in most European countries. Growth alone cannot reduce debt ratios, so primary surpluses will be needed.
Debt ratios rise in the US, Germany and France and fall in Spain and Japan. US debt is projected to exceed Italy's level as early as 2030. Italy and the UK see slight declines.
Risks are skewed to the upside for debt. A combined shock to rates and growth would weigh most on countries with the largest financing needs, starting with the US and Japan.

US: the primary deficit is estimated to widen to -4.2% of GDP in 2026 from -3.2% in 2025, mainly because of lost tariff revenue as reciprocal tariffs are refunded and gradually replaced. It narrows to -3.5% in 2027.

US: the interest rate-growth gap closes almost entirely by 2032. Nominal growth falls from nearly 6% to about 4% and the effective interest rate rises as debt is refinanced. A larger share of short-term issuance speeds up the pass-through to debt service costs.

US: the debt ratio rises from under 125% of GDP in 2025 to over 140% in 2032. Annual increases are limited to 1pp in 2026 and 2027 and exceed 3pp from 2030. Debt rises in every scenario. The best case is still above 130% in 2032, a combined growth and rate shock takes it toward 160%, and a rate shock alone takes it above 145%.

US yields: the curve has shifted sharply upward and is positively sloped across all maturities. The 2-year reflects expectations of tighter monetary policy driven by the conflict in Iran. Long yields are pushed up by strong US growth, competition for capital from AI investment needs, and a shift in the investor base from institutions to short-horizon buyers.

Germany: the primary deficit widens significantly in 2026-2027 because of infrastructure and defence spending allowed by relaxed fiscal rules. The apparent interest rate rises from 1.93% in 2026 to 3.16% in 2032, while nominal growth falls from 4.2% to 2.8%, so the interest-growth gap turns unfavourable from 2030. Debt reaches 80% of GDP in 2032 versus 62.7% in 2025 and rises even in the favourable scenario.

France: the primary deficit is too high to stabilise debt, and the effort needed to stabilise the ratio by 2032 is nearly 4pp of GDP (EUR 140bn). The effective interest rate exceeds nominal growth from 2028. New debt is issued near 5% while maturing debt carries under 1%.

France: the baseline has debt at 124.5% of GDP in 2032, assuming a primary surplus of 1.5% of GDP that month. Delaying consolidation by one year adds 2pp to the 2032 debt ratio. BNP does not expect expenditure cuts before 2028 because the government lacks a majority in the National Assembly.

France: the OAT-Bund spread reached 160bp at end-October (175bp at the peak). Long rates have risen more than short rates, which BNP reads as market concern about the government's consolidation target. Average debt maturity is just over 8 years.

Italy: the primary balance moves from -3.5% in 2023 to a surplus of 1.2% expected this year and 2% by 2032. Debt is 137% of GDP in 2026, falling to 133.7% in 2032. The effective interest rate rises from 3.12% in 2026 to 3.67% in 2032 and exceeds nominal growth from 2028, so significant primary surpluses are needed.

Spain: the primary surplus rises to +1% of GDP by 2032 and nominal growth stays above the apparent interest rate throughout. Debt falls from 100.5% of GDP in 2025 to 88% in 2032, below 90% as early as 2030. Only the combined rate and growth shock brings debt back above 100% from 2031.

UK: the primary balance returns to surplus from 2028 (2024: -3.1%, 2026e: -1.1%). The apparent rate rises from about 3.5% in 2025 to nearly 4.5% by 2032 and exceeds nominal growth from 2029. Debt falls from 103% of GDP in 2027 to 97% in 2032. About 23% of UK debt is inflation-indexed, which exposes interest costs to energy shocks.

Japan: the primary balance worsened to -1.2% of GDP in 2026 and is projected at more than -2% in 2027, partly because of the suspension of the consumption tax on food. Debt falls from 205% of GDP in 2025 to 187% in 2032, but the pace of decline slows from 6pp in 2026 to under 1pp from 2030. A combination of weaker growth and higher rates would be enough to jeopardise the government's goal of reducing the ratio.

risk_factors: A combined interest-rate and growth shock would weigh most on countries with the highest financing needs, starting with the US and Japan.
US debt rises in every scenario, with a combined growth and rate shock taking it toward 160% of GDP by 2032.
France's consolidation depends on a National Assembly majority that the government lacks. A one-year delay adds 2pp to the 2032 debt ratio.
Italy's debt stabilisation is sensitive to growth, interest rates and the primary balance.
Spain's debt exceeds 100% of GDP again from 2031 only in the combined rate and growth shock.
UK debt is vulnerable to slower growth and to energy shocks through its 23% share of inflation-indexed debt.
Japan's debt reduction depends on the favourable rate-growth gap and is exposed to weaker growth combined with higher rates.
charts_described: Chart: US yield curve at 04/11/2026 versus Iran pre-conflict (27/02/2026), the June 2022 inflation peak and Dec 2019. The text says the curve has shifted sharply upward and is positively sloped across all maturities.
vol_and_positioning: US investor base is shifting from institutional investors to short-horizon buyers, which amplifies the rise in long-term yields.
The ECB is raising rates gradually, so short-term rate increases in France remain moderate while long-term rates rise more.
geopolitical: Conflict in Iran (pre-conflict reference date 27/02/2026) pushed up the 2-year US yield through expectations of tighter monetary policy and lifted yields across Europe.
Conflict in the Middle East accelerated the rise in French interest rates and added to the rebound in inflation expectations in advanced economies.
Energy crisis and energy shock: temporary support measures in the UK and Spain raise near-term deficits, and UK inflation-indexed debt exposes interest costs to energy prices.
US reciprocal tariffs are being refunded and gradually replaced, which cuts tariff revenue.

theme_stances.key_argument: Debt issued at low rates is being refinanced at current rates, so interest payments rise in all countries by 2032.
theme_stances.evidence: Interest payments are set to rise in all countries

theme_stances.key_argument: US primary deficits persist with no consolidation on the policy agenda, so debt rises in every scenario.
theme_stances.evidence: fiscal consolidation does not appear to be on the policy agenda

theme_stances.evidence: the current government does not have the necessary majority
